# Fingerprint canonicalisation vectors — provenance

**These vectors were NOT generated by this SDK. Do not regenerate them from .NET code.**

`fingerprint.json` is the cross-port specification and test suite for
`MachineFingerprint`, shared verbatim by all eight Tamga SDKs. Its `fingerprint`
values were produced by an **independent SHA-256 implementation**, not by any SDK — a
fixture an SDK produced can only prove that SDK agrees with itself, which is precisely
how a fleet-wide misreading of the `.machine` wire format stayed green in CI for two
years while no SDK could open a file the server actually emitted.

Read `_spec` in the file itself. It is the normative text; this document only records
why the file is here and which parts bite hardest in C#.

## The rule being pinned

```
canonical   = "tamga-fingerprint-v1" <US> join(<US>, sort_bytewise(["label=" + trimmed_value]))
fingerprint = lowercase_hex( SHA-256( UTF-8( canonical ) ) )        // 64 chars
```

`<US>` is a display placeholder in the JSON's `canonical` field for **U+001F**, the
ASCII unit separator, emitted as the single byte `0x1f`. Hash the real byte, never the
five-character string `<US>`.

## What this helper deliberately does NOT do

**It does not read hardware identifiers.** What identifies a machine is a product
decision — a cloned VM template shares them, a container has none, a replaced
motherboard changes them — and no default is right for both a desktop app and a
Kubernetes sidecar. The measured defect it *does* fix: all eight SDKs sent the caller's
string byte-for-byte, and the server stores `fingerprint TEXT NOT NULL` with no length
limit, no `CHECK` and no normalisation, unique per `(license_id, fingerprint)`. So
`"ABC-123"`, `"abc-123"` and `" ABC-123 "` were three machines on three seats.

**It does not Unicode-normalise, and that is a constraint rather than an oversight.**
.NET has `String.Normalize`, so adding NFC here would be one line. Do not. NFC is
unavailable without a new dependency in Rust and Go, and in C11 it would mean ICU or
hand-rolled Unicode tables inside a library whose whole selling point is having none. A
rule eight ports cannot implement identically is worse than no rule: it would yield two
fingerprints for one machine depending on which SDK the application was written in,
silently consuming two seats. Adding it would make .NET the outlier that disagrees with
the other seven. Callers whose values can arrive in more than one normal form must
normalise before calling — which `MachineFingerprint`'s own XML docs tell them.

## The three invariants, and the vector pair that pins each

| invariant | vectors |
|---|---|
| order-independence | `two_sorted` == `two_unsorted` |
| whitespace equivalence | `whitespace_trimmed` == `single` |
| case preservation | `case_preserved` **!=** `single` |

Case folding is deliberately absent: lowercasing a base64 or hex identifier corrupts it.

## The C#-specific trap: sorting

The sort is **bytewise ascending on the UTF-8 bytes of the whole `label=value`
component**. That is not what .NET's default string comparison does.

- `Array.Sort(string[])` / `List<string>.Sort()` / `string.CompareTo` are
  **culture-sensitive**. Measured on net8.0/ICU: `"Disk=x"` vs `"arch=y"` compares
  `+1` under the current culture and `-1` bytewise, so the default sort produces
  `arch=y, Disk=x` where the spec requires `Disk=x, arch=y`. Any mixed-case label set
  diverges.
- `StringComparer.Ordinal` **cannot** diverge from a UTF-8 byte sort for any input this
  type accepts, so there is nothing to pin. Labels are unique and ASCII-printable and
  `=` is ASCII, so the deciding byte between two components is always below `0x80` —
  inside the labels, or at the `=` terminating the shorter one. A value's bytes never
  reach the comparison, which is the only place UTF-16 code units and UTF-8 bytes
  disagree. tamga-js measured 8 732 016 valid pairs with zero divergence. **Do not write
  a test asserting the difference**: it is green for the wrong reason and the mutation
  survives. (Note also that UTF-8 byte order and code-point order are the same thing by
  construction, so "bytewise vs. code-point" is not a distinction either.) The
  implementation compares bytes directly because that is the rule as written, not
  because `Ordinal` would be wrong.

The two mutations that genuinely bite — here and in every sibling port — are **sort key
= whole `label=value` component vs. label only** and **case-sensitive vs.
case-insensitive sorting**. `fingerprint.json`'s own vectors discriminate neither:
`many`'s four labels sort identically under every comparer. `MachineFingerprintTests`
therefore adds two supplementary orderings **derived from the stated rule, not from this
implementation's output** — a mixed-case pair (`Disk=x` before `arch=y`) and a prefix
pair (`mac-1=x` before `mac=y`, because `-` is `0x2D` and `=` is `0x3D`) — asserting on
`Canonicalize` output only. They invent no fingerprint constant.

This repo already carries a hard-won fix for the same class of mistake: see
`CanonicalJson.Utf8OrdinalComparer` in `Proof.cs`, added after an offline-proof
field-ordering deviation from the server's `BTreeMap` was found in a `security-reviewer`
pass (`d13ca72`).

## Rejections throw; they are never repaired

Stripping a control character or deduplicating a repeated label would map two different
inputs onto one seat, which is the bug this helper exists to prevent. All eight
`rejected` cases must throw. The suite asserts each one by name.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `_spec` | the normative algorithm, validation rules and rationale |
| `vectors[].components` | ordered `[label, value]` pairs as the caller supplied them |
| `vectors[].canonical` | the canonical string, with `<US>` standing in for `U+001F` |
| `vectors[].fingerprint` | the expected 64-character lowercase hex digest |
| `rejected[].reason` | why the input is a caller bug rather than something to fix up |
